newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analysts see Q1 German GDP stronger despite ills.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Q1 German GDP stronger despite ills.

text.p: Germany's economy is expected to show greater strength in the first quarter than in the preceding quarter, despite continued worries about the labour market and the construction sector, private economists said on Tuesday.

Average expectations for first-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) data, due to be released on Thursday, are for an increase of 0.4 percent from the previous quarter, and 2.7 percent from the year-earlier quarter, according to a Reuters poll of 10 German economists.
The economics ministry, which rounds GDP data to the nearest half-percentage-point, said last month first-quarter GDP would be up 0.5 percent from the previous quarter.
In the fourth quarter of 1996, GDP was up 0.1 percent from the previous quarter, and up 2.2 percent from a year earlier.

"GDP is growing somewhat more strongly than we expected at the start of the year," said Nikolaus Keis of Bayerische Vereinsbank. "The seasonal recovery in the construction sector started a little earlier than last year."
Armin Kayser of SBC Warburg agreed. "Apparently the improvement in the labour market has already begun. Strong increases in industrial production are lifting economic output."
The analysts' forecasts ranged from 0.2 to 0.5 percent quarter-on-quarter growth, and from 2.4 to 3.0 percent year-on-year.
Some observers were less sanguine about the labour market and construction sectors, and few believed the economy would reach the government's target of 2.5 percent economic growth for the full year.
"The main question is not how strong economic growth is, but how bad the labour market remains. It is still burdened by structural problems," said Lothar Hessler of Trinkaus Capital Management.
"The (negative) trend that set in there early this year is not temporary. The most important thing would be for the labour market to become more flexible," Hessler said.

Stronger growth is badly needed if Germany is to come close to meeting the debt and deficit requirements for European monetary union this year, the key year for deciding what countries will participate in EMU at the January 1999 start.
A weak economy depresses the government's tax revenues while high unemployment boosts outlays for jobless benefits, widening the deficit.

"We see GDP at this level (0.4 percent), because the construction slump was not quite as deep as last year," said Adolf Rosenstock of IBJ Deutschland. "But growth won't reach 2.5 percent this year, because domestic demand is still very weak. We expect 2.25 percent."
